title: Ἀλώπηξ ἐξογκωθεῖσα τὴν γαστέρα
titleEn: The Fox with the Swollen Belly
part: The Fox with the Swollen Belly (Chambry 30)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 30. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἀλώπηξ λιμώττουσα, ὡς ἐθεάσατο ἔν τινι δρυὸς κοιλώματι ἄρτους καὶ κρέα ὑπό τινων ποιμένων καταλελειμμένα, ταῦτα εἰσελθοῦσα κατέφαγεν.
sentences.tr: Alōpēx limōttousa, hōs etheasato en tini dryos koilōmati artous kai krea hypo tinōn poimenōn kataleleimmena, tauta eiselthousa katephagen.
sentences.l: A fox, famishing, when she beheld in a certain hollow of an oak loaves and meat left behind by some shepherds, having gone in, ate them up.
sentences.i: A starving fox saw loaves and meat that some shepherds had left in the hollow of an oak; she went in and ate it all.
sentences.n: The opening is word for word that of the fox and the grapes (fable 32): Ἀλώπηξ λιμώττουσα, ὡς ἐθεάσατο… — the collection reuses its openings freely. καταλελειμμένα is a perfect passive participle with ὑπό and the genitive of the agent, 'having been left behind by'. The κατα- of κατέφαγεν is perfective: she ate them right up.

sentences.t: Ἐξογκωθεῖσα δὲ τὴν γαστέρα, ἐπειδὴ οὐκ ἠδύνατο ἐξελθεῖν, ἐστέναζε καὶ ὠδύρετο.
sentences.tr: Exonkōtheisa de tēn gastera, epeidē ouk ēdynato exelthein, estenaze kai ōdyreto.
sentences.l: But having been swollen as to her belly, since she could not get out, she was groaning and lamenting.
sentences.i: But her belly had swelled, and since she could not get out again, she groaned and wailed.
sentences.n: τὴν γαστέρα is the accusative of respect: the passive participle says she 'was swollen', and the accusative says where — a construction English handles with 'in' or 'as to'. The two imperfects leave her groaning on and on.

sentences.t: Ἑτέρα δὲ ἀλώπηξ τῇδε παριοῦσα, ὡς ἤκουσεν αὐτῆς τὸν στεναγμόν, προσελθοῦσα ἐπυνθάνετο τὴν αἰτίαν.
sentences.tr: Hetera de alōpēx tēide pariousa, hōs ēkousen autēs ton stenagmon, proselthousa epynthaneto tēn aitian.
sentences.l: But another fox, passing by that way, when she heard her groaning, having come up, inquired the reason.
sentences.i: Another fox passing that way heard her groaning, came up, and asked what the matter was.
sentences.n: ἀκούω takes the genitive of the person heard (αὐτῆς) and the accusative of the sound (τὸν στεναγμόν) — both at once here. τῇδε is a dative of the way by which, 'by this road'. The passer-by who asks the question is a fixed piece of Aesopic furniture.

sentences.t: Μαθοῦσα δὲ τὰ γεγενημένα ἔφη πρὸς αὐτήν· « Ἀλλὰ μένε τέως σὺ ἐνταῦθα, ἕως ἂν τοιαύτη γένῃ ὁποία οὖσα εἰσῆλθες, καὶ οὕτω ῥᾳδίως ἐξελεύσῃ. »
sentences.tr: Mathousa de ta gegenēmena ephē pros autēn· « Alla mene teōs sy entautha, heōs an toiautē genēi hopoia ousa eisēlthes, kai houtō rhāidiōs exeleusēi. »
sentences.l: And having learned the things that had happened, she said to her: « Well, you stay here for the time being, until you become such as you were when you went in, and so you will come out easily. »
sentences.i: When she had learned what had happened she said to her, « Then stay where you are for now, until you are as you were when you went in — and you will get out easily enough. »
sentences.n: ἕως ἄν with the subjunctive (γένῃ) sets an indefinite future limit, 'until such time as'. τοιαύτη … ὁποία is a correlative pair, 'of such a kind … as of what kind'; and ὁποία οὖσα εἰσῆλθες is literally 'being of what kind you went in', a participle where English wants a clause. τέως is 'meanwhile, for the present'.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι τὰ χαλεπὰ τῶν πραγμάτων ὁ χρόνος διαλύει.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi hoti ta chalepa tōn pragmatōn ho chronos dialyei.
sentences.l: The story shows that the hard things among affairs, time undoes.
sentences.i: The story shows that time undoes what is difficult.
sentences.n: The moral is in the present, not the usual gnomic aorist: διαλύει states a standing truth. The object comes first and the subject ὁ χρόνος is kept back to the last breath before its verb — the Greek keeps 'time' for the end.
